task_title: After Landing, Parking, and Securing (ASEL, AMEL)
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why each shutdown, postflight and securing step exists, how a pilot documents a discrepancy and what a pilot may and may not do about it, and you can teach a learner to park, shut down, inspect, secure the airplane and handle passengers on the ramp, spotting and fixing the errors learners make.
why: Situational awareness only ends when the airplane is safely and securely back at its tie-down or hangar [[24:38|AFH 2-1]], and a flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane is secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. This is the last Task of the course and the one you will teach at the end of every lesson, usually when you and your learner are tired. Learners copy their instructor's habits whether they mean to or not [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], so the way you finish each flight becomes the way they finish theirs.

prereading.what: After-landing checklist, parking, the engine shutdown list, postflight inspection, servicing and tie-downs. The core of this Task.
prereading.label: AFH 2-22 to 2-23

prereading.what: The ramp environment, passengers, refueling, exhaust blast, hand signals and the nearly invisible propeller.
prereading.label: AFH 2-14 to 2-17

prereading.what: Why the ignition goes OFF after shutdown and what a broken magneto ground wire means.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-16

prereading.what: In-flight discrepancies, deferral, removal and deactivation, preventive maintenance and the entry a pilot makes.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-9 to 9-10

prereading.what: Who decides the airplane is safe, who must fix discrepancies, and who may do and sign off preventive maintenance.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.7, 91.405, 43.3 to 43.9

prereading.what: Automatic checklist recitation, slips under time pressure, habit formation and the instructor as safety role model.
prereading.label: AIH 3-28 to 8-6

prereading.what: Security Identification Display Areas, briefing passengers, the Airport Watch number and showing your certificate to TSA.
prereading.label: AIM 2-3-15

warmup: Think first: your learner has just finished a good lesson. A friend of hers is in the back seat, your next student is waving from the FBO door, and the fuel truck is pulling up. In the next five minutes, what are the three things most likely to be skipped, who could get hurt or what could get broken, and what will you say or do to stop each one?

key_terms.def: The mixture position that stops fuel flow and shuts the engine down. The PHAK calls it the only way to stop an engine whose magneto ground wire has broken.
A brief turn of the ignition switch to OFF at idle during shutdown, to prove the switch really grounds the magnetos.
The wire that shorts the magneto to turn the ignition off. If it breaks, the engine can fire with the switch OFF.
A walkaround after shutdown and deplaning, looking for leaks, stains, damage and blocked inlets, plus oil and fuel servicing.
Anything wrong with the airplane that a pilot finds in flight or on the ground and reports to maintenance.
A log for writing up discrepancies. Under an MEL, AC 91-67A accepts it in place of the maintenance records if it is kept as part of the aircraft records.
Simple or minor preservation work and replacement of small standard parts without complex assembly, limited to the Part 43 Appendix A(c) list.
The signed maintenance record entry that lets an airplane fly again after work. After preventive maintenance a pilot needs at least a private certificate to give it.
A marking near the switch, control or indicator of a failed item, so the next pilot and the mechanic know its condition.
A device that holds the flight controls so wind cannot slam them while the airplane is parked.
Security Identification Display Area: a limited-access part of an airport where an airport-issued badge must be displayed.
The disk the propeller sweeps. Nearly invisible when turning, and the place where ramp injuries happen.

chunks.title: S1: Parking where the blast, the wind and the people allow

body.p: This lesson starts where the Private and Commercial lessons on this Task leave the runway: rollout, the runway exit and the after-landing checklist are taught there (PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A), and taxi in AI.V.D. Here you teach what happens on the ramp, and why. Remind the learner of one rule from those lessons: the after-landing checklist is done only after a complete stop beyond the runway holding position markings, unless the manufacturer calls for an item on the rollout [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
Parking is the first skill the evaluator sees (ACS AI.XIV.A.S1). The AFH guidance [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]:

bullets: Unless the spot is in a designated, supervised area, pick a location and heading that keep other airplanes' propeller or jet blast from striking yours unnecessarily.
Whenever possible, park headed into the existing or forecast wind. Tie-downs may not line up with the wind or leave much choice.
After stopping in the direction you want, let the airplane roll straight ahead enough to straighten the nosewheel or tailwheel.

body.p: Teach the reason behind each one, not just the rule:

head: Hazard
What the source says
What the learner checks before turning in
rows: Other airplanes' blast
Powerful aircraft can make exhaust blast or rotor downwash strong enough to make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]
Which nearby airplanes are running or may start, and where their tails point
Your own propeller
A propeller can throw objects to high speed, damaging property and injuring people on the ground [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
What is behind the tail as it swings into the spot, and how much power the turn needs
The ramp itself
Workers, passengers, trucks, aircraft and even stray people and animals share it, and the pilot is responsible for operating safely [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]
Who is walking, and where the passengers will step out
The rule
Careless or reckless operation on an airport surface used for air commerce is prohibited even when you are not flying [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(b)]]
Speed and power near people and property

body.p: Marshallers: the AFH says the exact set of signals matters less than every operation using a suitable, agreed-upon set, and at night the Emergency Stop signal is used for all stops [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner say the parking plan out loud before the last turn: "My blast goes toward the grass, the twin on the left is cold, wind is from the west, so I will park nose west, roll straight, and stop." Saying it out loud lets you hear a bad plan before it happens.

check.q: The tie-down rows face east, but the wind is from the west. Your learner asks whether she must hunt for a spot that faces the wind. What does the AFH say?
check.a: Park headed into the existing or forecast wind whenever possible, but the AFH accepts that tie-downs may not line up with the wind or leave much choice [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Then secure the airplane well.

chunks.title: K1 and S2: The shutdown flow and the reason for each step

body.p: Always use the airplane's AFM/POH shutdown checklist. The AFH lists important items that may be on it [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. A CFI applicant is expected to explain why each one is there. Where the sources give no reason, say so and send the learner to the POH.

head: Typical item (AFH order)
Why you teach it
rows: 1. Parking brake ON
Holds the airplane while the hands work the engine controls (application). It is released later, after chocks, per the POH [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
2. Throttle IDLE or 1,000 rpm
The AFH value [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; your POH may give another
3. Turbocharged: spool-down
Follow the manufacturer's spool-down procedure [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. The time comes from the POH
4. Magneto switch test

A momentary check at idle that the switch grounds properly in OFF [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. If the ground wire is broken, the engine could start when someone moves the propeller with fuel still in a cylinder [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
5. Propeller control HIGH rpm, if equipped
Listed [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; the AFH gives no reason, so use the POH
6. and 7. Avionics OFF, alternator OFF
Listed before the mixture [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; no reason is given in the sources
8. Mixture IDLE CUTOFF
Stops the engine. It is also the only way to stop an engine whose magneto ground wire is broken [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
9. Ignition OFF when the engine stops
A magneto needs no outside power, so with the switch left ON the engine can fire if the propeller is moved, even with the battery and master OFF [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
10. Chocks in, parking brake released per AFM/POH
11. Master switch OFF
12. Control locks and anti-theft locks

body.p: Add the ELT check to the flow if your POH lacks it: the AIM asks pilots to monitor 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown at the end of each flight [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: A good magneto check does not make the propeller safe. A faulty switch can sit in OFF and still let the magneto fire, so anyone touching a propeller should assume the ignition is on [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

body.p: Flow and checklist. The AFH says a checklist need not be a do-list: you can do the actions and then use the checklist to confirm them, but it is worthless if the pilot is not committed to using it. After landing, and engine shutdown and securing, are on its minimum list of checklist phases [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

callout.text: Hold, Prove, Starve, Kill, Keep: hold it (brake, idle), prove the mag ground, starve it (mixture cutoff), kill the switches (ignition, master), keep it (chocks, locks).

check.q: Your learner skips the magneto check: "the engine is about to stop anyway." What does the check protect against?
check.a: A broken magneto ground wire. With it, the switch reads OFF but the engine could start when someone moves the propeller [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. The check at idle finds it before anyone touches the propeller [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: the shutdown and securing lesson

head: When
What you do
rows: Ground briefing, early lessons

Walk through the POH after-landing, shutdown and securing checklists with the learner and give the reason for each item. Hazards and mitigations get their detailed discussion in the preflight and postflight briefings, not at a time when the learner is busy [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
First few flights
You park, shut down and secure while explaining each step and each reason. The learner watches your hands and eyes, not just the list
Next flights

The learner does it, touching each control and naming its reason. Watch for a recitation that runs ahead of the hands: the AIH warns that a checklist can become so automatic that the words are decoupled from the actions they should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Every flight
Insist on the correct technique from the start. Faulty habits are hard to correct later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]
After the securing

Postflight walkaround together, the learner writes up any discrepancy, then the debrief. The AFH light sport chapter does the complete postflight inspection after the airplane is shut down, tied down and secured, has squawks noted and reported to maintenance, and calls for a training debriefing [[24:349|AFH 17-15]]

body.p: You are the model for this Task more than for any other. Learners treat the instructor as a role model whose habits they imitate, and safety talk means little if the instructor does not show it every time [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. If you hop out while the propeller is still turning, leave the control lock in your flight bag or skip the walkaround to catch your next student, your learner will too.

Checklist usage and aviation security are both on the AIH list of common special emphasis items instructors should cover [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. This Task is where both show up at the end of every lesson.

callout.text: Application: early in training, end the lesson at the tie-down with one question: "Is the airplane ready for the next pilot?" The learner answers by walking you through the locks, covers, tie-downs, fuel, oil and the squawk sheet.
Do not start the debrief with the engine running or the propeller still turning. Teaching at an inappropriate time can create a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Your learner always shuts down well with you aboard. Why does the AIH say you should insist on the correct flow from the very first lesson?
check.a: It is the instructor's job to insist on correct techniques and procedures from the outset, because proper habits are much easier to build at the start than faulty ones are to correct later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

chunks.title: S3: Postflight inspection and servicing, taught as the next preflight

body.p: After engine shutdown and deplaning the passengers, the pilot does a postflight inspection: a walkaround of the general condition of the airplane [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

bullets: Cowling: oil or fuel streaks near and around it, and excessive oil discharge around the oil breather.
Under the wings and other fuel tank locations: fuel stains.
Landing gear and tires: damage. Brakes: leaking hydraulic fluid.
Cowling inlets: obstructions. [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]

body.p: Servicing [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]:

bullets: Check the oil and bring it to the AFM/POH level.

Oil: check it on every preflight and recheck with each refueling; if oil use increases or suddenly changes, qualified maintenance personnel should investigate [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. That is why the amount added belongs in the write-up.

Add fuel based on the airplane's immediate use. If it will sit inactive, filling the tanks is good practice to prevent water condensation inside them; if another flight is planned, fuel to that flight's planning requirements.
Full tanks also slow the aging of rubber fuel tanks and tank sealant [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].
Fuel weight matters for the next pilot's weight and balance: aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]] [[1:246|PHAK 10-2]].

body.p: Refueling: take the passengers out of the airplane and watch the refueling, to make sure the right fuel and quantity go in and that caps and cowls are secured afterward [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. The same goes for oil: the AFH says not to leave fuel and oil to line service without the pilot's oversight [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. The fuel grade colors and the grounding and bonding sequence are taught in CA.XI.A; point the learner there.

Why rushing this step fails: the AIH uses this photo for mistakes made under pressure, such as a cursory inspection to save time with a problem showing up later [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. The more hurried the work, the more slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

callout.text: The ACS element asks the applicant to document discrepancies and servicing requirements (ACS AI.XIV.A.S3). Teach the learner to write down oil added and fuel needed, not just broken parts, so the next pilot knows what was done.

check.q: The airplane will sit for a week. Your learner wants to leave the tanks half full to "keep it light." What do you teach?
check.a: Filling the tanks of an airplane that will be inactive is good practice to prevent condensation [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], and keeping them full slows the aging of rubber tanks and sealant [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. Weight is planned before the next flight.

chunks.title: K2: Documenting discrepancies: who must know, and what to write

body.p: Teach the learner the chain of responsibility first. A discrepancy that stays in the pilot's head never gets fixed.

head: Rule
What it means for the learner
rows: The PIC decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight, and must discontinue the flight when an unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural condition occurs
The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the airplane airworthy, including compliance with Part 39 (ADs)

The owner or operator has the airplane inspected as Part 91, Subpart E prescribes and, between required inspections, has discrepancies repaired as Part 43 prescribes. They can only fix what someone reports
In-flight discrepancies: use the AFM/POH procedures in the air. Maintenance deferrals are not used for them
After the airplane is shut down, tied down and secured, any squawks or discrepancies are noted and reported to maintenance

body.p: Where it goes. The AFH says only that squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]]. The written-record rules in AC 91-67A are for airplanes operated under an MEL: a failure after takeoff is handled with the AFM/POH procedures and recorded in the aircraft maintenance records, and before the next takeoff the item is repaired or deferred under the MEL [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]]. An inoperative item gets an entry in the maintenance records, and because some operators do not carry the logbooks aboard, a discrepancy record or log is an acceptable alternative if it is kept as part of the aircraft's records [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]]. The PHAK's MEL example also uses an entry in the maintenance record or discrepancy record provided for that purpose [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Without an MEL, the sources name no format; teach the system your school or owner uses.

What a useful write-up says (application): the item, what it did, when and under what conditions, what the pilot already checked, the date, the tach or Hobbs time and the pilot's name. Compare "radio bad" with "COM 1 transmits are weak and broken per tower and ground at three airports today; COM 2 normal with the same headset."
Placards finish the job. AC 91-67A says each inoperative item is placarded to inform and remind the flightcrew and maintenance personnel of its condition [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.3]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner write the squawk, then read it back to them as if you were the mechanic: "Where would I start looking?" If they cannot answer, the write-up is not finished.

check.q: Your learner reports a squawk to the front desk and asks whose job it is to get it fixed. What do you teach?
check.a: The owner or operator has discrepancies repaired as Part 43 prescribes between required inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]] and is primarily responsible for airworthiness [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. The PIC's part is to report it, and to decide before each flight whether the airplane is safe [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

chunks.title: K2: What a pilot may and may not do about a discrepancy

body.p: The full rules for flying with inoperative equipment (91.213(d), MELs, the KOEL and the Part 43 Appendix A list) are taught in AI.III.B and AI.V.A. At the end of a flight the learner needs to know who may act:

head: Action
Who may do it
Source
rows: Decide the airplane is or is not safe to fly
The pilot in command
Preventive maintenance (simple or minor preservation, small standard parts, no complex assembly)

The holder of a Part 61 pilot certificate other than a sport pilot certificate, on an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot and not used under Part 121, 129 or 135. A sport pilot may do it only on an aircraft she owns or operates that has a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category. (Paragraphs (h) and (i) add narrow Part 135 exceptions.) To operate an aircraft includes piloting it
Which jobs count

Only the Part 43 Appendix A(c) list, such as replacing bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights, or replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap. Limits matter: only landing light wiring circuits may be troubleshot and repaired, and hose connections may be replaced except hydraulic connections
Approve the airplane for return to service after that work
A person holding at least a private pilot certificate, after doing that preventive maintenance under 43.3(g)
The record entry

Description of the work, date completed, the name of the person who did it if someone else approves it, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it. The signature approves only the work done
Fly it afterward
Nobody, until it has been approved for return to service and the entry is made
Remove an inoperative item
Removal is always maintenance: certificated maintenance personnel, recorded under Part 43
Deactivate an inoperative item
Can be as simple as a pilot pulling a circuit breaker; complex deactivation needs a certificated, appropriately rated maintenance person. Always placarded INOPERATIVE
Decide a deferred item is not a hazard
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot, or a person certificated and rated to maintain the aircraft
Get the deferred item fixed
The owner or operator, at the next required inspection
Make sure inoperative instruments or equipment on the discrepancy list are placarded
The owner or operator

body.p: Student and recreational pilots. A student pilot certificate is one of the Part 61 pilot certificates [[60:194|14 CFR 61.5(a)(1)]], and 43.3(g) excludes only sport pilots [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. But 43.7(f) requires at least a private pilot certificate to approve the return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], so a student or recreational pilot cannot sign off the work. The PHAK says student, sport and recreational pilots may not do preventive maintenance at all [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]; teach the CFR text (see the CFI notes). In practice, teach the student to write it up and leave the fix to someone who can sign for it.
A failed magneto grounding check is not a pilot fix. The PHAK says to stop the engine with the mixture and have the system checked by a qualified AMT [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

callout.text: Maintenance means inspection, overhaul, repair, preservation and replacement of parts, and it excludes preventive maintenance [[60:10|14 CFR 1.1]]. If the job is not on the Appendix A(c) list, it is not the pilot's job [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: Your renter asks why 43.3(g) covers her at all, since she does not own the club airplane. What do you show her?
check.a: 43.3(g) covers an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]], and to operate an aircraft means to use, cause to use or authorize to use it for air navigation, including piloting it [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. The club's own rules may still limit who does maintenance.

chunks.title: S4 and R2: Securing the airplane and airport-specific security

body.p: The airplane is hangared or tied down, the flight controls secured, and security locks in place [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Teach the reason for each piece:

head: Item
What the AFH says [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
rows: Chains
Not flexible. Do not pull them taut; leave some movement to prevent airframe structural damage
Ropes
Flexible. They may be reasonably cinched to the tie-down rings
Control locks
Flight controls secured; a rudder gust lock where used
Covers
Pitot tube covers and cowling inlet covers
Other
Window sunscreens and propeller security locks add safety and security
Hangar
Leave enough space so the airplane cannot hit the hangar, another aircraft or a vehicle, and inspect it for damage after hangaring

body.p: Airport-specific security (ACS AI.XIV.A.R2). Each airport sets its own access rules, so teach the learner to find out, not to guess:

bullets: A SIDA is a limited-access area that needs a badge. It can include movement or parking areas; a Secured Area, where airline passengers board, is always a SIDA. Going into one without authorization and displayed ID is prohibited [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
If unsure where a SIDA is, contact the airport authority. Airports with one have a description and boundary map available [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].
Pilots or passengers seen entering a SIDA without proper ID may be reported to TSA or airport security and face civil and criminal fines and prosecution, so brief passengers [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Report suspicious activity through AOPA's Airport Watch Program, 866-427-3287. 49 CFR 1540 requires you to show your airman or medical certificate to TSA on request [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].
Passengers not under the pilot's direct supervision need an escort for safety and ramp security [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

body.p: Security at the start of a flight (planning, NOTAMs, TFRs) is covered in AI.V.A. At the end of a flight it is physical: locks on, gates closed behind you, passengers escorted out.

callout.text: Application: at a new airport, have the learner ask the FBO before leaving the airplane: Is this ramp part of a SIDA? What is the way out? Ropes or chains? Then they secure the airplane and lead the passengers out themselves.

check.q: Your learner cinches both tie-down chains as tight as she can "so it can't move in the wind." What do you teach?
check.a: Chains are not flexible, so they are left with some movement to prevent structural damage; only ropes are reasonably cinched [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

chunks.title: R3: Getting passengers off the airplane and keeping track of them

body.p: The rules keep passengers in their seats until the airplane stops. No pilot may move an airplane on the surface unless the PIC has made sure each person on board was told to fasten the safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]], and each person must keep it fastened in an approved seat during movement on the surface [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. AC 91-73B suggests asking passengers to keep a sterile cockpit from the start of landing preparations until the airplane is safely stopped at the terminal [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].
Why the propeller is the main ramp risk:

bullets: A spinning propeller can be lethal if it strikes someone [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

It is nearly invisible. The AFH's hand-propping section warns that people have been seriously hurt and killed walking or reaching into the propeller arc to remove chocks, reach the cabin or move toward the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. The same arc is beside the door your passengers use.
Even stopped, treat it as live: a faulty switch can be OFF and still let the magneto fire [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

Other airplanes count too. Powerful aircraft make blast and rotor downwash [[24:52|AFH 2-15]], and the rotating beacon program is voluntary, so do not rely on a beacon alone to know whether an engine is running [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

body.p: Monitoring passenger movement. Passengers may have little ramp experience, so the pilot cautions them to move only as directed, and anyone not under the pilot's direct supervision gets an escort [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Passengers come out before refueling [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

head: Moment
What you teach the learner to say or do (application)
rows: Before engine start
Brief the exit: "Stay seated until I say. Then walk back past the wing, away from the propeller, and wait for me."
Taxi in
Belts stay on, sterile cockpit until stopped [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]
Shutdown
Repeat the brief, and open the door only after the propeller has stopped
On the ramp
Lead the group, keep them in sight, and keep them away from running airplanes and SIDA gates until they are off the ramp

callout.text: Watch the learner, not just the passengers. A learner focused on a checklist may not see a passenger open a door. The pilot is responsible for safe operation on the ramp [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

check.q: As the engine winds down, the back-seat passenger opens his door and starts to step out toward the front of the wing. Your learner is reading the checklist. What do you do and teach?
check.a: Stop him: the propeller arc is nearly invisible, and the AFH records serious injuries and deaths of people walking into it toward the cabin or tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Afterward teach the learner to brief the exit and direct passenger movement [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

chunks.title: R1: Activities and distractions at the end of a lesson

body.p: The end of a lesson is crowded: radio calls, a strange ramp, passengers who want out, a lineman, a fuel truck, the next student, a phone. What the sources say:

bullets: Pilots have a limited capacity for information; past it, new information is missed or pushes out other tasks, and distraction and fixation make it worse [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
Many cockpit distractions begin as a minor problem, and fatigue, stress and overload narrow a pilot's attention [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

Cell phones and other devices are discouraged during taxi, and everyone on board should turn them off [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]]. Nonessential actions wait until clear of all runways [[7:7|AC 91-73B 7d(13)]].
On the ground, the pilot can stop the airplane, deal with the issue and then resume taxi [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Time pressure causes slips: the more hurried the work, the more slips. Working deliberately at a comfortable pace reduces errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].
Raise awareness when errors are known to happen, such as changes in routine and time pressure, or when defenses are weak, such as fatigue [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

head: Distraction
Mitigation you teach (application unless cited)
rows: Lineman or fuel truck arrives during shutdown
Finish the shutdown first; refuel only with passengers out and the pilot watching [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]
Next student waiting at the wing
Wave them back; securing comes before the handoff
Passenger questions on the taxi in
"Hold that until we stop" [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]
Phone buzzes
Off during taxi [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]]; read it after the airplane is secured
Checklist interrupted
Stop, then restart that section from the top
The instructor is rushed
Your own schedule is a distraction too; learners imitate what you do [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]

body.p: The manufacturer's checklists are a basic defense against errors, and schools and clubs may add their own procedures to them [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. If your school has a securing checklist, teach it alongside the POH list.

check.q: On the taxi in, your learner's phone buzzes in her pocket and she reaches for it. What does AC 91-73B say?
check.a: Cell phones and other devices are discouraged during taxi, and everyone aboard should turn them off to prevent distractions [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]]. Read it after the airplane is secured.

body.p: The ACS asks you to describe the common errors (K3) and to analyze and correct them (S5). Each row below comes from what the sources say should be done.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Parking in another airplane's blast
Spot right behind a running or soon-to-start airplane
Pick a spot and heading clear of others' blast [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]
Nosewheel or tailwheel left cocked
Airplane stopped mid-turn in the spot
Roll straight ahead a little before stopping [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Shutdown from memory
No checklist out, items done in a different order each time
Flow, then the checklist to confirm [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]
Rushed recital
Words faster than the hands; wrong lever touched
Touch, name, give the reason [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Magneto check skipped
Key goes straight from BOTH to OFF at shutdown
Brief OFF check at idle [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Ignition left on
Key at BOTH after the engine stops
Ignition OFF when the engine stops [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Door opened with the propeller turning
Passenger or learner climbing out at idle
Shut down first; passengers move only as directed [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]
Postflight skipped or rushed
Learner heads for the FBO after the locks go on
Walkaround after deplaning, every flight [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]
Verbal squawk
"Tell maintenance the radio is weird"
Note it and report it to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]]; under an MEL, an entry in the maintenance records or discrepancy log [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]]
Fixing beyond the rules
Learner offers to tighten, adjust or remove something not on the Appendix A(c) list, or a student offers to sign
Report it; pilots do only Appendix A(c) work, and at least a private certificate is needed to sign [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]
Tie-down chains pulled taut
Chains drum-tight
Leave some movement [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Locks and covers forgotten
Controls free, pitot open
Control locks, covers, security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]
Passengers left to wander
Group heads across the ramp alone
Escort them [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]; brief SIDA rules [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]]

body.p: When the learner makes one of these errors, ask why it happened and what would prevent it, and do not let them keep practicing the wrong way [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Many of them look like slips, and the most common slip is simply neglecting to do something [[25:84|AIH 3-33]] (application), which is why the checklist and a deliberate pace are the main fixes.

check.q: You see the key still at BOTH after the propeller stops and the learner reaching for the master switch. Which error is it, and what makes it dangerous?
check.a: Ignition left on. The AFH turns it OFF when the engine stops [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], because the magneto needs no outside power: anyone moving the propeller could start the engine, even with the master OFF [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

scenario.title: Last lesson of the day on a busy FBO ramp
scenario.setup: It is 1730. Your learner, a private pilot working on her instrument rating, lands at a towered airport with airline service after a dual flight in the club airplane. Her brother is in the back seat. On the taxi in she mentions that the attitude indicator tumbled briefly in the climb. The FBO ramp has a turboprop starting two rows over, a lineman with wands, and a fenced airline ramp next to it. Your next student is due at 1800 and the airplane will sit at this field for the weekend.

questions.q: The lineman waves her toward a spot directly behind the turboprop that is starting. What do you teach?
questions.a: The pilot is responsible for the airplane on the ramp [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Unless the spot is in a designated, supervised area, pick a location and heading clear of other airplanes' blast [[24:60|AFH 2-23]], since blast from powerful aircraft can make a light airplane uncontrollable [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. Stop, and settle a better spot with the lineman using agreed-upon signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

questions.q: Her brother wants to hop out as soon as they stop to photograph the airliners. What do you have her brief?
questions.a: Stay belted and seated until the propeller stops; then move only as she directs, with an escort if not under her direct supervision [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. The propeller arc is nearly invisible, and the AFH records people hurt and killed walking into it toward the cabin or tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Entering the airline ramp, if it is a SIDA, without ID can bring fines and prosecution [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15]].

questions.q: During shutdown the magneto check is normal, but she pulls the mixture before turning the avionics off. Is that an error?
questions.a: The AFH lists avionics and alternator off before the mixture but gives no reason, and says to use the AFM/POH checklist [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Check the POH order with her; if it matches the AFH, have her redo it per the checklist and use the checklist to confirm the flow [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

questions.q: What should she do about the attitude indicator?
questions.a: In flight it was handled with the POH procedures; deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Now she notes it and reports it to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]] so the owner can have it repaired [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]; if the club airplane has an MEL, the failure is recorded in the maintenance records before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]]. A useful entry says what happened, when and in what conditions (application).

questions.q: How does she service and secure an airplane that will sit all weekend?
questions.a: Oil to the POH level; fill the tanks to prevent condensation since it will be inactive [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Tie it down (chains with some slack, ropes reasonably cinched), control locks, covers and security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

questions.q: At 1750 she starts rushing to get you to your next student. What do you do?
questions.a: Slow her down: hurrying produces slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], and the flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Your example counts; learners copy their instructor's habits [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

skills.do: Park in an appropriate area, considering the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS AI.XIV.A.S1). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees you pick a spot and heading clear of other airplanes' blast, into the wind when possible, roll straight to stop, and explain each choice and its hazard aloud as you would to a learner.
skills.practice: On every taxi in, say the parking plan out loud before the last turn: blast, wind, people, property [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

skills.do: Complete the appropriate checklist(s) (ACS AI.XIV.A.S2). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees you run the POH after-landing, shutdown and securing checklists while explaining why each item is there, including the magneto grounding check at idle, mixture to idle cutoff, and ignition OFF when the engine stops.
skills.practice: Read your training airplane's POH shutdown list and write one reason beside each item, marking those the sources do not explain [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

skills.do: Conduct a postflight inspection and document discrepancies and servicing requirements, if any (ACS AI.XIV.A.S3). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees a real walkaround (cowling, breather, tank areas, gear, tires, brakes, inlets), oil and fuel servicing decisions, and a clear written entry for anything found.
skills.practice: After every flight, write a squawk or a "no discrepancies, oil added" line as if a mechanic will read it [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

skills.do: Secure the airplane (ACS AI.XIV.A.S4). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees chocks, tie-downs fitted to their type, control locks, covers and security locks, and hears the reason for each, for example why chains keep some slack.
skills.practice: Secure the airplane while explaining it to a friend, then ask them to point out anything left undone [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.XIV.A.S5). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator may play a learner who leaves the key ON, opens the door at idle or writes a vague squawk; you name the error, its hazard and the fix, citing the source.
skills.practice: Have another instructor applicant act out the errors in the common errors table while you spot and correct each one [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

quiz.q: Turning into a gravel tie-down, your learner adds a burst of power while the tail swings toward a parked car. What hazard does the AFH name?
options: Power at low taxi speed overheats the brakes, which may fade on the next taxi
Gravel drawn into the cowling inlets can block the cooling air the engine needs on the ground
The propeller can throw objects fast enough to damage property and injure people
A burst of power on the ground can overspeed a fixed-pitch propeller
quiz.why: A propeller or other engine thrust can accelerate objects to substantial velocities, damaging property and injuring people on the ground [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; pick the spot and heading first [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

quiz.q: Your learner checks out in a turbocharged airplane. Which shutdown item does the AFH add for it?
options: Shut down straight from cruise power so oil keeps flowing through the hot turbo
Leave the alternator on for five minutes after the engine stops
Set the mixture full rich and hold 1,700 rpm before cutoff
Observe the manufacturer's spool-down procedure
quiz.why: If turbocharged, observe the manufacturer's spool down procedure [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. The time comes from the AFM/POH.

quiz.q: In the AFH shutdown list, what happens to the parking brake?
options: Never set, because brakes left on can bind or freeze on the ramp
Released before the magneto check so the airplane can roll straight
Set ON first, then released per the AFM/POH once the chocks are in
Left set overnight in place of tie-downs when the wind is calm
quiz.why: The AFH list starts with the parking brake ON and, after the mixture and ignition, installs chocks and releases the parking brake in accordance with the AFM/POH [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

quiz.q: Late in the day your learner flies a club airplane she has not used before. Why does the AIH say to be extra alert for errors in her shutdown?
options: A different airplane always calls for a new demonstration of every procedure by the instructor
Errors are known to happen with changes in routine and time pressure, and fatigue weakens defenses
Learners make more errors in the afternoon because their short-term memory is already full
The AIH says to cancel the lesson when a learner changes airplanes after a long day
quiz.why: Raise awareness when operating in conditions under which errors are known to happen (changes in routine, time pressure) or when defenses are compromised (fatigue, lack of recent practice) [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

quiz.q: Element S3 of this Task asks the applicant to conduct a postflight inspection and document discrepancies and what else, if any?
options: Hobbs and tach times
Passenger names and weights
Fuel and oil receipts
Servicing requirements
quiz.why: S3: conduct a postflight inspection and document discrepancies and servicing requirements, if any (ACS AI.XIV.A.S3). Oil added and fuel needed belong in the write-up.

quiz.q: An airplane operated under an approved MEL carries no logbook on board. Under AC 91-67A, where can your learner record a newly inoperative item?
options: In a discrepancy record kept as part of the aircraft's records
In the remarks column of the learner's own pilot logbook
On a sticky note on the panel until a mechanic can see it
Nowhere else, as long as the item is placarded INOPERATIVE near its switch
quiz.why: Under an MEL, an inoperative item needs a maintenance record entry; since some operators do not carry logbooks aboard, a discrepancy record or log is an acceptable alternative if kept as part of the aircraft's records [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]].

quiz.q: A sport pilot renter flies the club's J-3 Cub, which has a standard airworthiness certificate. She wants to replace a cracked position light lens herself. What do you tell her?
options: Yes: the lens is on the Appendix A(c) list, so any Part 61 pilot who flies the Cub may do it
No: a sport pilot may do preventive maintenance only on a light-sport category aircraft
Yes, but a pilot with at least a private certificate must approve the return to service
Yes, as long as her CFI watches the work and endorses her logbook for it afterward
quiz.why: 43.3(g) excludes sport pilots except on an aircraft they own or operate that has a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The PHAK notes the Cub, though in the LSA category, was certificated as a normal aircraft [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

quiz.q: Besides tie-downs and the control lock, which items does the AFH suggest to further enhance a parked airplane's safety and security?
options: Wing covers, a battery tender, an engine preheater and locking fuel caps on both tanks
Cowl flaps open, fuel selector OFF, wheel pants removed and a tail stand
Pitot tube cover, cowling inlet covers, window sunscreens and a propeller lock
Static port tape, an oil filler lock, a cabin dehumidifier and wing tie bars
quiz.why: Consider pitot tube covers, cowling inlet covers, rudder gust locks, window sunscreens and propeller security locks to further enhance safety and security [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

quiz.q: Between back-to-back lessons you sometimes leave the control lock in your bag. What does the AIH say your learners will likely do?
options: Imitate the habit, because learners see the instructor as a role model
Report it, because learners are trained to speak up about safety lapses
Copy it only when they fly that same airplane on their own later
Ignore it, because learners follow the POH checklist rather than the instructor
quiz.why: Learners consider their instructor a role model whose habits they imitate, consciously or not, and safety advice means little if the instructor does not demonstrate it consistently [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

quiz.q: Taxiing into the tie-down row, your learner asks how her last landing looked. Per the AIH, what do you do?
options: Keep her eyes outside and save it for after shutdown; teaching at the wrong time can create a hazard
Take the controls and debrief the landing while you taxi in
Give a full critique now, while the landing is fresh in her mind
Have her stop on the taxiway with the engine running for the debrief
quiz.why: Avoid creating a hazard by teaching at an inappropriate time, and discuss hazards and risk mitigation in detail during preflight and postflight [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your school flies under an approved MEL. A strobe fails in flight; the next lesson in that airplane is in an hour. Under AC 91-67A, what must happen before that next takeoff?
options: Nothing, since MEL relief carries over from the flight on which the strobe failed
The failure is recorded, then the strobe is repaired or deferred under the MEL
The next pilot may take off and decide once airborne whether to defer it
An IA must inspect the airplane, since an in-flight failure voids the MEL
final_quiz.why: MEL relief does not apply to failures after takeoff: the crew uses the AFM/POH procedures, a record is made in the maintenance records, and before the next takeoff the item is repaired or the PIC follows the MEL deferral procedures [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]].

final_quiz.q: Your private-pilot learner replaces a worn front seat belt in the club airplane she flies and writes only "Replaced L seat belt" with her initials. What must the entry also show?
options: The tach time, the new belt's part number and an IA's countersignature
Her medical certificate class and the date she last flew this airplane as PIC
A Form 337 reference, since belts are cabin safety equipment
The date, and her signature, certificate number and kind of certificate
final_quiz.why: Replacing safety belts is preventive maintenance [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)(14)]]. The entry needs the description, the date of completion, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving the work [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

final_quiz.q: On the postflight you both see red fluid at the left brake and a damp hydraulic line fitting. Your private-pilot learner offers to fix it. What do you teach?
options: Write it up: the list lets pilots replace hose connections, except hydraulic ones
She may replace the fitting, since hose connections are preventive maintenance
She may tighten the fitting and fly, since a small leak is only a servicing item
Leave it for the next annual, since brakes are not part of the postflight check
final_quiz.why: The AFH postflight checks the brakes for leaking hydraulic fluid [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Appendix A(c) allows replacing any hose connection except hydraulic connections [[60:143|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)(21)]], so it goes to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your flight school adds its own securing checklist (covers, fuel order, squawk sheet) to the POH shutdown list. How does the RMH treat that?
options: As unapproved, since only the manufacturer's checklist may be used in the airplane
As an SOP that enhances the manufacturer's checklist, which is the basic defense
As a replacement for the POH list, which then no longer needs to be used
As legal only after the local FSDO has reviewed and approved it
final_quiz.why: The manufacturer's approved checklists are a basic defense, and many flight schools and flying clubs develop checklists and SOPs that enhance the manufacturer's procedures [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing in, your learner's panel light fails and she keeps troubleshooting it while a fuel truck crosses ahead. What does the AFH say about this?
options: A failed panel light must be fixed before the airplane may taxi further
Fixating on a minor failure displaces tasks of greater importance
Troubleshooting on the move is fine if the taxi speed stays at a walk
As an in-flight discrepancy it is handled first with the AFM/POH
final_quiz.why: Distraction and fixation impede processing; the AFH's example is a pilot fixating on an instrument light failure, which displaces tasks of greater importance [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. On the ground she can stop, deal with it, then resume [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner parks at an FBO on an airport with airline service and is unsure which areas are a SIDA. What is the best source?
options: The nearest airline gate agent working on the ramp
Ground control, which issues SIDA clearances to pilots on request by radio
The legend of the sectional chart for that airport
The airport authority, which has a description and boundary map
final_quiz.why: If unsure where a SIDA is, contact the airport authority; airports with a SIDA have a description and map of its boundaries available [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15]].

final_quiz.q: The airplane sits overnight, and a heavy three-passenger party has it at 0800. Your learner wants to top off now. What does the AFH say?
options: Always fill the tanks to the top to prevent condensation, whatever comes next
Never add fuel at the end of the day; fuel only before departure
Fuel to that flight's planning requirements, since another flight is planned
Leave the tanks low so the next pilot can choose the fuel load
final_quiz.why: Fuel is added based on the immediate use of the airplane; if another flight is planned, the tanks are filled to that flight's planning requirements [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Avgas weighs 6 pounds per gallon [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]].

final_quiz.q: After a night dual cross-country your learner wants to skip the walkaround because "it flew fine." What do you teach?
options: Skip it tonight and do a longer preflight tomorrow morning
Do it with a flashlight; the flight is not complete until the airplane is secured
Have the line service crew do it while you both leave
Only check the oil level, since that is the one postflight item the AFH requires
final_quiz.why: The postflight inspection follows shutdown and deplaning, and a flight is not complete until the engine is shut down and the airplane secured [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. A cursory inspection to save time can let a problem show up later [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

final_quiz.q: A private pilot renter replaced and gapped the spark plugs in the club airplane she operates under Part 91, and asks you, the CFI, to sign it off. What is correct?
options: She signs it herself, since she did the preventive maintenance and holds a private certificate
You sign it, since a flight instructor certificate covers maintenance sign-offs
Only an A&P mechanic may sign, because plugs are engine parts
The club owner signs, because the owner is responsible for airworthiness
final_quiz.why: Replacing and cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap is preventive maintenance [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]]. A person with at least a private certificate may approve the return to service after doing it under 43.3(g) [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], and the signature approves only the work done [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

final_quiz.q: As you shut down, the dispatcher radios that your next student is waiting, and your learner starts unbuckling with the checklist half done. What do you teach?
options: Skip to the master switch, since everything else on the list can wait until later
Let her go and finish the securing yourself after the next lesson
Finish the flow and checklist at a deliberate pace; hurrying produces slips
Read the rest of the checklist aloud while she climbs out
final_quiz.why: The more hurried the work, the more slips; working deliberately reduces errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Engine shutdown and securing is a phase that needs a checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

final_quiz.q: After the lesson the lineman offers to top off the oil while you both go inside to debrief. What does the AFH suggest?
options: The pilot watches that the right grade and quantity go in and the cap is secured
Let him do it unwatched, since line personnel are aviation professionals
Have him add a quart above the POH level to cover the next pilot's flight
Skip it tonight, since the oil level only matters on the next preflight
final_quiz.why: Do not leave fuel and oil to line service without the pilot's oversight; when oil is added, the pilot should monitor the quantity, quality and grade and see that the caps are secured [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. Oil goes to the AFM/POH level after flight [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

final_quiz.q: On the walkaround you find oil sprayed along the belly behind the breather tube. What does the AFH have the pilot look for there, and what follows?
options: Fuel venting from overfilled tanks; drain some fuel until the stain stops
Normal breather venting after a hot flight; wipe the belly and fly
A loose oil filler cap only; tighten it yourself and fly tomorrow
Excessive oil discharge; note it and report it to maintenance
final_quiz.why: Inspect around the oil breather for excessive oil discharge [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]].

final_quiz.q: Why does AC 91-67A require each inoperative item to be placarded?
options: So the FAA can track equipment failures across the fleet
To show the item may not be repaired until the next annual inspection
To inform and remind the flightcrew and maintenance personnel
To let any pilot remove the item without a record entry
final_quiz.why: Each inoperative item must be placarded to inform and remind the flightcrew and maintenance personnel of its condition [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.3]].

takeaways: The flight ends at the tie-down: shutdown, postflight, write-up and securing are part of every lesson.
Teach the reason for each shutdown step; say plainly where the sources give none and use the POH.
Magneto check at idle, mixture to cutoff, ignition OFF when stopped, and treat every propeller as live.
Write discrepancies down for the mechanic: what, when, conditions. The PIC reports; the owner fixes.
Pilots do only Appendix A(c) work, and approving the return to service takes at least a private pilot certificate.
Passengers stay seated until the propeller stops, then move only as directed, escorted off the ramp.
Your own end-of-lesson habits are the ones your learners will copy.
cfi_notes: The AFH lists avionics and alternator OFF before the mixture, and propeller HIGH rpm, without giving reasons [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Do not invent one for the learner; check the POH and say so.
The AFH says the parking brake is released after chocks "in accordance with AFM/POH" [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Some POHs say little about it; teach the school's standard and why.

Student pilots: 43.3(g) does not exclude them [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] and a student pilot certificate is a Part 61 certificate [[60:194|14 CFR 61.5(a)(1)]], but 43.7(f) needs at least a private certificate to approve the return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. The PHAK says student, sport and recreational pilots are excluded from doing preventive maintenance [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]; that line does not match the current 43.3(g), which excludes only sport pilots (except on light-sport category aircraft). Teach the CFR, and know your school's rule; many schools forbid students from doing any maintenance.

Whether a student pilot counts as "certificated and appropriately rated" for the 91.213(d)(4) no-hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]] is not settled by these sources. Have a rated pilot or mechanic make it.
The sources give no format for a discrepancy write-up outside an MEL operation. The squawk content in this lesson is application; teach your school's form.

Adding engine oil is not on the Appendix A(c) list [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]], yet the AFH tells the pilot to bring oil to the AFM/POH level after flight [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] and describes line service adding oil under the pilot's oversight [[24:47|AFH 2-10]]. The PHAK's sample preventive maintenance entry is "changed oil (Shell Aero-50) at 2,345 hours" [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], so it treats an oil change as preventive maintenance, but no source says whether topping off is servicing or preventive maintenance. Follow the operator's practice and record oil added.

The AFH line about people killed walking into a nearly invisible propeller arc comes from its hand-propping section [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. It fits deplaning passengers, but say where it comes from. Likewise, the AC 91-67A discrepancy-record rule [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.2]] is written for MEL operations; for other airplanes the AFH only says squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]].
Do the walkaround with the learner, not for them. A learner who never sees you skip it will not skip it [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

This Task overlaps PA.XII.A and CA.XI.A (runway exit, fueling, hand signals), AI.V.C (propeller safety) and AI.III.B (inoperative equipment). Teach those details there and keep this lesson on the end-of-flight habit.
gaps: Exact shutdown order, idle rpm, turbo spool-down time, and whether the parking brake stays set: AFM/POH only.
No source gives a reason for turning avionics and the alternator off before the mixture, or for propeller HIGH rpm at shutdown.
No source gives a standard discrepancy write-up format for Part 91 airplanes without an MEL.
Airport-specific security rules (gate codes, escort rules, badge areas) come from each airport authority, not the handbooks.
The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for any S element of this Task.

activities.title: True or false: shutdown reasons
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In the AFH shutdown list, the propeller control goes to low rpm, if equipped.
cards.why: False. The AFH sets the propeller control to HIGH rpm, if equipped [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

cards.s: The AFH shutdown list sets the throttle to IDLE or 1,000 rpm.
cards.why: True. Item 2: throttle IDLE or 1,000 rpm; your AFM/POH may give another value [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

cards.s: The AFH explains that avionics are turned off before the mixture to protect them from voltage spikes.
cards.why: False. The AFH lists the item but gives no reason [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. Check your POH.

cards.s: The last item on the AFH shutdown list is installing control locks and anti-theft security locks.
cards.why: True. Item 12: secure, install control locks and anti-theft security locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

cards.s: In the AFH list, the master switch goes OFF before the chocks are installed.
cards.why: False. Chocks go in (item 10) before the master switch goes OFF (item 11) [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

cards.s: The AIM asks pilots to monitor 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown at the end of each flight.

activities.title: Point your learner at the postflight spots
activities.intro: Drag each part name to its place on the AIH photo. Then name the AFH postflight check for each part that has one.

activities.title: Servicing numbers for the write-up
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The tanks were filled to 52 gallons, but the next flight, planned for tomorrow, needs only 30 gallons. How many pounds heavier is the airplane than if fuel had been added only for that flight?
items.why: (52 - 30) gal x 6 lb/gal = 22 x 6 = 132 lb [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]]. If another flight is planned, the AFH fuels to that flight's planning requirements [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

items.q: Your learner's write-ups show 1 quart of oil added after each of three flights of 1.8, 2.2 and 2.0 hours. On average, how many flight hours per quart is the engine using?
items.why: 1.8 + 2.2 + 2.0 = 6.0 hours; 6.0 hours / 3 quarts = 2.0 hours per quart. Recording oil added is what makes this visible [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

items.q: Last month the same engine used 1 quart every 6.0 hours. Now it uses 1 quart every 2.0 hours. How many times as much oil per hour is it using now?
items.why: (1 / 2.0) / (1 / 6.0) = 0.5 / 0.1667 = 3. If consumption increases or suddenly changes, qualified maintenance personnel should investigate [[24:47|AFH 2-10]].

items.q: Tomorrow's flight needs 38 gallons by its fuel plan, and the tanks hold 14 gallons now. How many pounds does the fuel your learner orders add?
items.why: 38 - 14 = 24 gal; 24 gal x 6 lb/gal = 144 lb [[22:67|W&B Handbook 7-7]]. Fuel to the planned flight's requirements [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

activities.title: A discrepancy from cockpit to fix
activities.intro: Put the life of a discrepancy in order, from the moment it appears to the next flight. Then tap Check.
steps: In flight: handle it with the AFM/POH procedures, not a deferral
After shutdown: note it and report it to maintenance
The owner or operator has it repaired as Part 43 prescribes
The person approving the work signs the record entry, approving the return to service
The next pilot may fly the airplane

activities.title: Who may do it?
activities.intro: Tap each action, then the person the cited source gives it to.
buckets: Any Part 61 pilot except a sport pilot, on an airplane they own or operate (not used under Part 121, 129 or 135)
A pilot with at least a private pilot certificate

items.t: Replace a defective cotter key on a Part 91 airplane
Clean and grease the landing gear wheel bearings
Approve the return to service after doing that preventive maintenance
Troubleshoot and repair a broken circuit in the strobe light wiring
Fix a magneto ground fault found at shutdown
Have the airplane inspected as Part 91, Subpart E requires
Make sure inoperative instruments on the discrepancy list are placarded

activities.title: Ramp moment to the right move
activities.intro: Tap a ramp or securing moment, then the move the sources call for.

pairs.l: A ramp you have never used
pairs.r: Review the airport diagram and keep it at hand

pairs.r: The pilot supervises loading and security
May be reasonably cinched to the rings
Checked and brought to the AFM/POH level

activities.title: Finishing a lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: Your learner, a new private pilot, flies the club airplane with her father in the back. The airplane will sit until Monday. You decide as the lesson ends.

steps.s: Taxiing in, ground control gives a long instruction just as her father starts talking and a fuel truck crosses ahead. What do you have her do?
options: Keep rolling and ask ground to repeat it later
Speed up to get past the fuel truck first
Stop the airplane, sort it out, then resume the taxi
Answer her father, then read back from memory
steps.why: On the ground the pilot has the option to stop and resume taxi after addressing an issue [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]; passengers can be asked to keep a sterile cockpit until the airplane is stopped [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

steps.s: At the spot, with the engine still running, her father wants to get his bag out of the baggage door behind the wing. What does she say?
options: "Wait until the engine stops; then I will get the bag with you."
"Go ahead, just walk around the front of the wing."
"Go now, the propeller is at idle and easy to see."
"Open your door so you are ready, but stay seated."
steps.why: The pilot supervises baggage and tells passengers to move only as directed [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]; the propeller arc is nearly invisible [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

steps.s: The magneto check is normal. She then moves the key to OFF before pulling the mixture. What do you say?
options: Nothing, the order does not matter
Tell her to turn the master off first next time
Tell her to leave the key on BOTH for the next pilot
Ask her to check the POH order: mixture to cutoff stops the engine, ignition OFF once it stops
steps.why: The AFH order is mixture to idle cutoff, then the ignition OFF when the engine stops [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; use the POH checklist to confirm [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

steps.s: On the walkaround she finds fresh fuel stains under the right wing. What now?
options: Wipe them off; they are probably from fueling
Note it and report it to maintenance so they can find the source
Fix the leak by tightening the fittings herself
Leave a note on the seat for the next renter
steps.why: Fuel stains under the wings are an AFH postflight item [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; squawks are noted and reported to maintenance [[24:349|AFH 17-15]], and fittings are not on the preventive maintenance list [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

steps.s: It is windy and the airplane sits until Monday. How does she secure it?
options: Ropes left loose so they do not stretch
Chains with some slack, control lock and covers, tanks filled
Chains as tight as possible, no control lock needed
Parking brake set overnight instead of tie-downs
steps.why: Chains not taut, controls secured, covers and locks [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]; filling the tanks of an inactive airplane prevents condensation [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].
